title: Learning one by heart
hook: learning one shabad by heart means it's there when you need it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ragi, who chooses the right shabad for the hour, and your line: the right song. A ragi knows hundreds of shabads. Today, the gift of knowing just one.

Phone numbers used to live in people's heads. Now they live in phones, and mostly that's fine, until the battery dies at the wrong moment. The same is true of words that steady us. A line saved in an app is no help in an MRI machine, or at three in the morning, or in the half second before you say something you'll regret. Only what's inside you is there then.
screen: `PHONE NUMBERS WE USED TO KNOW.` → `MEMORY HANDED TO OUR POCKETS.` → `ONLY WHAT'S INSIDE IS THERE.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi, to learn something by heart is to make it kanth, literally, to put it in the throat. It's a lovely image: the words live where your voice comes from, ready to rise. Before printed books, a handwritten copy of the scripture was a precious thing, and Sikh tradition remembers Gurbani carried kanth, in memory. Children learned the Japji Sahib by repeating it after a grandparent each morning. Sikhs who keep Nitnem often know their daily prayers by heart, the Nitnem you've met this year: Japji, Jaap, the Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. Some know long hymns like Sukhmani Sahib. And the Granth itself treats the Word as something held inside. Guru Amar Das says, on Ang sixty-seven, in paraphrase: the Guru's bani is the light in this world; by grace it comes to dwell in the mind. That's the hope: not words you look up, but words that live in you. Learning by heart changes how a shabad works. Read on a page, it's information. Known by heart, it's company. It comes back on its own while you're driving or washing up, and each time you understand a little more. You don't need a whole bani to start. Two lines, really known, are enough to be there when you need them.
screen: `KANTH: KEPT IN THE THROAT.` · `GURBANI CARRIED IN MEMORY.` · `THE BANI IS LIGHT IN THE MIND.` · `TWO LINES, REALLY KNOWN.` · then, large: `BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Choose two lines, the shabad you picked for your home two days ago or any line from this path, and say the first aloud slowly three times, then once with your eyes closed. Do the same with the second, then say both together; if you lose a word, peek and try again, no rush. If you pray, let the lines be your prayer.
Kanth, the throat: to make a shabad kanth is to learn it by heart, so the words are inside you, ready, when there's no book and no phone.
Your line: by heart. Known by heart, a line becomes company. That's day six hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs often learn their daily prayers and favorite shabads by heart, often as children repeating after a parent or grandparent, so they can recite them anywhere.
